What exactly is gluconeogenesis?

blocks.x: Gluconeogenesis is the synthesis of brand-new glucose from non-carbohydrate starting materials — things like lactate, pyruvate, glycerol, citric acid cycle intermediates, and certain amino acids. The name says it all: gluco (glucose) + neo (new) + genesis (creation) — literally, "making new glucose."

Imagine a household that normally buys bread from the shop (dietary carbohydrates) or pulls a loaf from the freezer (stored glycogen). But when the shop is closed and the freezer is empty — during a long fast, starvation, or after a hard day's labour — someone in the house has to actually bake bread from raw flour and other ingredients lying around: leftover rice water (lactate), cooking oil residue (glycerol), even protein scraps (amino acids). That emergency baker is gluconeogenesis, and the "bakery" is mainly the liver.

Why does the body bother? Because glucose is the non-negotiable fuel for several tissues: the brain and central nervous system, the testes, red blood cells (erythrocytes), and the kidney medulla. The body needs about 160 g of glucose per day, and the brain alone burns through roughly 120 g of that. Stored glycogen holds around 190 g — just about one day's worth of reserve. Beyond that, gluconeogenesis has to take over.

sections.title: Which organs do this, and when does it kick in?

blocks.x: The liver is the major site of gluconeogenesis in mammals — think of it as the main bakery for the whole household.
The kidney cortex is a secondary site, running at only about 1/10th of the liver's capacity — a smaller neighbourhood bakery that helps out when needed.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — when the "emergency baker" is called in

blocks.x: This baker doesn't work every day — only when needed: during prolonged fasting, starvation, or after intense exercise has drained glycogen reserves. When blood glucose starts dropping (hypoglycaemia), the brain — which relies on glucose as its primary fuel, with fat-derived ketone bodies only as a backup during prolonged starvation — signals that supply must be restored quickly. Gluconeogenesis also does double duty as a clean-up crew: it clears metabolites like lactate, glycerol, and propionate that would otherwise accumulate in the blood.

sections.title: Gluconeogenesis is NOT just glycolysis in reverse

blocks.x: Gluconeogenesis closely resembles the reversed glycolytic pathway — but it isn't a complete reversal. Of the 10 reactions in glycolysis, 7 are reversible and are reused directly by gluconeogenesis. But 3 steps are irreversible — catalyzed by hexokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), and pyruvate kinase — and simply cannot run backward. Gluconeogenesis has to build entirely new detours around each of these three roadblocks, using 4 unique enzymes found only in specific tissues (mainly liver and kidney).

blocks.x: Picture glycolysis as a road with three strict one-way streets (hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase). You simply cannot drive back through a one-way street. So to go the opposite direction, the city has to build three completely separate bypass roads around those junctions. Everywhere else, the same two-way streets (the 7 reversible steps) work fine in either direction.

blocks.cap: Because oxaloacetate can't cross the mitochondrial membrane directly, it's disguised as malate for the trip, then converted back once inside the cytosol.

blocks.x: In the mitochondrion, pyruvate carboxylase carboxylates pyruvate into oxaloacetate, requiring ATP and the coenzyme biotin. Since oxaloacetate can't cross the mitochondrial membrane, it's converted to malate, shuttled into the cytosol, and converted back to oxaloacetate there. Finally, PEP carboxykinase decarboxylates and rearranges it into phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), using GTP and Mg²⁺.

PEP is hydrated to 2-phosphoglycerate (enolase, run in reverse), converted to 3-phosphoglycerate (phosphoglycerate mutase), then phosphorylated using ATP to form 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (phosphoglycerate kinase).

1,3-bisphosphoglycerate is reduced to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP) using NADH as the electron donor (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase). Some GAP is isomerized to DHAP (triose phosphate isomerase), and the two are combined by aldolase to form fructose-1,6-bisphosphate — the two 3-carbon halves reunited into one 6-carbon molecule.

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1) removes a phosphate, requiring Mg²⁺. This bypasses the irreversible PFK-1 step from glycolysis. Note: this enzyme is absent in smooth muscle and heart muscle, and it's also a major regulatory checkpoint.

Fructose-6-phosphate is isomerized to glucose-6-phosphate (phosphohexose isomerase), then glucose-6-phosphatase removes the final phosphate to release free glucose, which can now enter the bloodstream. This bypasses hexokinase. This final enzyme is present mainly in liver and kidney, but absent in muscle, brain, and adipose tissue — which is exactly why those tissues can't release glucose into the blood themselves.

sections.title: Gluconeogenesis isn't free

blocks.x: The overall equation for building one glucose molecule:

Buying bread from the shop (dietary glucose) or grabbing a stored loaf (glycogen breakdown) is cheap and quick. But baking fresh bread from scratch — grinding your own flour, sourcing yeast, running the oven — costs real time, effort, and money. That's exactly why gluconeogenesis "costs" 6 high-energy phosphate bonds and 2 NADH per glucose made — it is clearly not simply glycolysis running backward for free.

sections.title: Where does the "flour" for this baking come from?

blocks.x: When oxygen is limited — hard exercise, or cells like erythrocytes that have no mitochondria at all — cells run anaerobic glycolysis and produce lactate. This lactate travels to the liver, gets converted back to glucose via gluconeogenesis, and the glucose travels back out to the muscles and red blood cells to be broken down again. This round-trip loop is called the Cori cycle — like a delivery truck that keeps shuttling flour back and forth between the bakery and the market stall, never letting either side run completely dry.

blocks.x: When fat cells break down stored triacylglycerols, they release free fatty acids and glycerol. Glycerol travels to the liver, gets phosphorylated by glycerol kinase, then oxidized into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) — which slots directly into the gluconeogenesis pathway. It's like using leftover cooking oil scraps as a starter ingredient for the next batch of bread.

blocks.title: The precursor that does NOT work — fat

blocks.x: This is one of the most heavily examined points in the whole topic: fatty acids cannot be converted into glucose. Even-chain fatty acids are broken down into acetyl-CoA, and the reaction that makes acetyl-CoA from pyruvate (pyruvate dehydrogenase) is irreversible. Once a carbon has entered as acetyl-CoA it can be burned in the Krebs cycle, but there is no route back to pyruvate — so it can never become glucose. Every acetyl-CoA that enters the cycle also leaves as two CO₂, so no net carbon is available for glucose. The one exception: odd-chain fatty acids finish with a 3-carbon propionyl-CoA, which is converted to succinyl-CoA and enters the Krebs cycle as a genuine anaplerotic input — that carbon can leave as oxaloacetate and become glucose. The glycerol backbone of a triacylglycerol is also glucogenic (see above). So the fully correct answer is: the fatty acid chains of ordinary fat cannot make glucose; the glycerol head and odd-chain tails can. This is exactly why prolonged starvation forces the body to break down muscle protein for glucogenic amino acids — despite having plenty of fat still stored.

Certain amino acids can be broken down into citric acid cycle intermediates (like alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, and fumarate), which are then converted to oxaloacetate — the very substrate PEP carboxykinase needs. This is why, during starvation or in diabetes mellitus, the body starts breaking down muscle protein for amino acids — sacrificing muscle tissue to keep making glucose for survival.

sections.title: Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are like a see-saw

blocks.x: These two pathways are reciprocally regulated — when one is switched up, the other is switched down, so the cell never wastefully runs both directions at once. A high AMP level signals low energy and a need for ATP; a high ATP or citrate level signals the cell already has plenty of energy and building blocks.

blocks.cap: When glycolysis's "weight" (AMP, F-1,6-BP) rises, it tips down and gluconeogenesis rises — and vice-versa.

blocks.x: Pyruvate kinase is inhibited by ATP and alanine, but activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate — so high energy charge shuts glycolysis off, while glycolytic intermediates keep it going. Pyruvate carboxylase is stimulated by acetyl-CoA (excess building blocks push glucose-making forward) but inhibited by ADP (low energy charge shuts gluconeogenesis off). PEP carboxykinase is also switched off by ADP.

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase is inhibited by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP) and AMP — and interestingly, these same two molecules have the opposite effect on PFK-1 (they activate it). It's the same signal read in reverse by each pathway's key enzyme.

sections.title: Glucagon vs. Insulin — the outside signals

blocks.x: Beyond the cell's own internal fuel gauges, two hormones from outside the liver cell issue broader instructions.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — two managers with opposite instructions

blocks.x: Think of glucagon and insulin as two shift managers who never agree. When blood glucose is low, glucagon steps in: it lowers F-2,6-BP levels in the liver, which turns PFK-1 down (less glycolysis) and turns fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase up (more gluconeogenesis) — a fast, short-term response. Insulin gives the exact opposite instructions when glucose is abundant. Over the longer term, these two hormones also control how many "staff" (enzyme molecules) are on duty at all. Glucagon induces the production of PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, glucose-6-phosphatase, and certain aminotransferases — while it represses glucokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase. Insulin generally does the reverse.

Bottom line: a high glucagon-to-insulin ratio increases the liver's capacity for gluconeogenesis and decreases its capacity for glycolysis. When blood glucose is low, glycolysis drops and gluconeogenesis rises to compensate. Another booster: during starvation, excessive fat breakdown (lipolysis) causes acetyl-CoA to build up in the liver, which allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase — directly promoting glucose production.

sections.title: Why does this matter for real patients?

blocks.x: Insulin normally inhibits gluconeogenesis. Without adequate insulin production or sensitivity (as in diabetes), gluconeogenesis runs unchecked, worsening hyperglycemia. Metformin, a first-line type 2 diabetes drug, suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis by activating AMPK, which also improves insulin sensitivity.

Clearing ethanol from the body requires two oxidation steps (via alcohol dehydrogenase, then aldehyde dehydrogenase), both consuming NAD⁺. This causes NADH to pile up, which pushes the lactate dehydrogenase reaction toward making more lactate instead of pyruvate. With less pyruvate available and NAD⁺ in short supply, gluconeogenesis is inhibited — leading to both lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia after heavy drinking.

Preterm infants have limited glycogen and fat stores, and their gluconeogenic enzymes are often expressed at sub-optimal levels. This leaves them at high risk of hypoglycemia, since they can deplete energy stores quickly without being able to mount a proper backup response.

sections.title: Key takeaways

items: Gluconeogenesis builds new glucose from non-carbohydrate sources — lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids — mainly in the liver, with the kidney cortex as a smaller backup.

It is not simply glycolysis reversed: 7 steps are shared and reversible, but 3 irreversible glycolytic steps are bypassed using 4 dedicated enzymes — pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase.
Making one glucose molecule costs 6 high-energy phosphates (4 ATP + 2 GTP) and 2 NADH — gluconeogenesis is energetically expensive.
The Cori cycle recycles lactate from muscle/RBCs back into glucose via the liver.

Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are reciprocally regulated at two coordinated control points, refined further by glucagon (promotes gluconeogenesis) and insulin (promotes glycolysis, inhibits gluconeogenesis).

Clinically, dysregulated gluconeogenesis is central to diabetes (excess glucose output), alcohol-induced hypoglycemia (NADH pile-up blocks the pathway), and hypoglycemia in preterm infants (underdeveloped enzyme systems).

items.d: Pyruvate → Oxaloacetate, in the mitochondrion. Needs biotin + ATP.
Oxaloacetate → PEP, needs GTP. OAA must first shuttle out of the mitochondrion as malate.
PEP is converted back up through the shared reversible glycolytic steps to Fructose-1,6-BP.
Glucose-6-P → free Glucose. Only in liver and kidney — releases glucose into the blood.
